paper.title: The Danish EQ-5D-5L Value Set: A Hybrid Model Using cTTO and DCE Data
paper.journal: Applied Health Economics and Health Policy
paper.code_data_availability: "Availability of data and material/Code availability Available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. …

registers.role: sample frame and population benchmark: supplied contact information on a randomly chosen representative sample of the adult Danish population and the population distributions used to assess representativeness in Table 1

registers.name_in_paper: registers on the use of health and social services (mentioned as part of Statistics Denmark's holdings, not used for any variable in this study)
EQ-VT version 2.1 valuation interview (EuroQol Valuation Technology): cTTO and DCE tasks - the study's own primary data
registers.role: treatment (health states valued) and outcomes (cTTO values, DCE choices)

linkages: Invitations were sent to individuals' secure national digital mailbox linked to the personal registration number (CPR) supplied by Statistics Denmark.
Each respondent's cTTO observations and DCE observations are linked by respondent in the hybrid model.

sample.unit_of_observation: Respondent x health state for cTTO (10 per respondent); respondent x choice pair for DCE (7 per respondent)
selection_rules: Statistics Denmark drew a randomly chosen sample representative on age (> 18 years), gender, education and geographical region; contact information on 4585 individuals was supplied, in blocks of approximately 500, each block meeting the representativeness requirements.
Invitations sent by personal letter to the secure national digital mailbox; reminders by mailbox, home address and/or telephone.

A Danish market research company was added half-way through the study period, inviting its panel under the same representativeness principles; panel members who had participated in a health survey within the last 6 months were not eligible.
1052 interviews were carried out between October 2018 and November 2019.
5 interviews dropped: two interviewers were asked to leave as they were not sufficiently available.
12 interviews dropped due to software issues, respondents withdrawing consent, or cognitive/emotional issues.
21 participants dropped for not contributing both cTTO and DCE data, leaving 1014 interviews.
For cTTO modelling: cTTO data for health states respondents identified in the feedback module as inappropriately ranked were dropped (n = 712), leaving 9428 observations.
No exclusions were made due to logical inconsistencies between EQ-5D-5L health states or non-trading.
No additional exclusion criteria were applied for the DCE data (7098 observations).
sample.n_observations: 10,140 cTTO observations (9428 used for cTTO modelling) and 7098 DCE observations

construction_notes: 86 EQ-5D-5L health states were valued by cTTO, in blocks of ten balanced on severity: one 'mild' state (four dimensions at level 1, one at level 2), eight 'moderate' states and the most severe state 55555; each respondent was randomly assigned one block and the order of states was randomised.
196 DCE pairs in 28 blocks of seven, similar in level sum score; block assignment, pair order and left-right positioning randomised.

cTTO: conventional TTO for states better than dead (value x/t between 0 and 1) and lead-time TTO for states worse than dead (value (x - 10)/10, between -1 and 0); values range from -1 to 1 in 0.05 increments because the smallest tradeable time was 6 months.
Observed cTTO values are censored at -1 by construction of the EQ-VT; the Tobit and hybrid models account for this censoring.
Modelling was used to extend the 86 directly valued states to all 3125 EQ-5D-5L states; no interaction effects were included or investigated.
Table 2 beta coefficients are utility decrements: the value of a state is 1 minus the sum of its dimension-level decrements (example: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439).

Quality control used the EQ-VT QC tool with four cTTO flags (no explanation of the 'worse than dead' task, under 3 min on the cTTO example, logical inconsistency where 55555 is valued at least 0.5 higher than the lowest rated state, under 5 min on the ten cTTO tasks).

claims.statement: In the heteroscedastic censored hybrid model chosen for the Danish EQ-5D-5L value set, mobility at level 2 carries a utility decrement of 0.041 relative to level 1.

treatment.label: mo2: mobility at level 2 of the EQ-5D-5L health state being valued (regular dummy, level 1 omitted)

definition.value: Regular dummy equal to 1 when the EQ-5D-5L health state presented to the respondent has the mobility dimension at severity level 2; the omitted category is level 1 (no problems) on that dimension. The EQ-5D-5L has five dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) each with five severity levels.

timing.value: Presented to the respondent during the computer-assisted personal interview (October 2018 - November 2019); each respondent valued ten cTTO health states and seven DCE pairs in one interview.

outcome.label: Utility decrement (β) of an EQ-5D-5L dimension level in the final Danish EQ-5D-5L value set, estimated jointly from cTTO and DCE data

definition.value: Table 2 reports β coefficients that "should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life"; a health state's value is 1 minus the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels (worked example, p. 586: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439). The underlying elicited quantity is the observed composite time trade-off value of the health state, on a scale from − 1 to 1 in 0.05 increments (1 = full health, 0 = dead), censored at − 1; the model is estimated on heteroscedastic censored hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data, the model chosen for the final Danish value set.

timing.value: Elicited in the valuation interview itself; the cTTO task values living ten years in the health state, with lead-time TTO adding a further ten years for states considered worse than dead.

units.value: EQ-5D-5L utility decrement, in units of the value scale on which 1 = full health and 0 = dead

estimand.target_population: The adult (18+) Danish general population, whose preferences the value set is intended to represent.

population.description: 1014 adults (18+) from the Danish general population interviewed in the Danish EQ-5D-5L valuation study, each valuing ten EQ-5D-5L health states by cTTO and seven pairs by DCE.
population.selection: Statistics Denmark drew a randomly chosen sample representative on age (> 18 years), gender, education and geographical region and supplied contact information on 4585 individuals, invited in blocks of about 500; a Danish market research company panel was added half-way through, selecting respondents by the same principles and excluding anyone who had taken a health survey in the previous 6 months. Of 1052 interviews carried out, 5 were dropped with two interviewers, 12 for software issues/withdrawn consent/cognitive or emotional issues and 21 for not contributing both cTTO and DCE data, leaving 1014.

identification.source_of_variation: Experimental variation in the EQ-5D-5L health states respondents were asked to value: a standardized blocked EQ-VT design in which 86 health states were valued in blocks of ten by cTTO (and 196 pairs in 28 blocks of seven by DCE), with respondents randomly assigned to a block and randomised order of states.

key_assumptions.assumption: Additive main-effects specification: the value of a health state is the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels, with no interactions between dimensions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the EQ-VT was designed for maximum power to identify main effects and that no interaction effects were included or investigated; the worked example on p. 586 adds decrements across dimensions. Not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The censoring of observed cTTO values at − 1, imposed by the construction of the EQ-VT, is correctly handled by the censored (Tobit) specification, and the distributional assumptions of that model hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5.1; the paper argues the Tobit model is conceptually preferred to the GLS model for this reason. The distributional form is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents' stated cTTO valuations measure the preferences of the adult Danish general population, and the achieved sample is representative of that population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 compares the study sample with Statistics Denmark figures for the adult Danish general population on gender, age, marital status, education, work status, income and region; the paper concedes slight under-representation of 18-24-year-olds and of the lowest educational level.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on respondent behaviour: cTTO observations for health states a respondent flagged in the feedback module as inappropriately ranked were dropped (712 observations), and respondents who did not contribute both cTTO and DCE data (n = 21) were dropped.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5 and Sect. 3.2. A sensitivity analysis reintroducing the 712 flagged observations left the estimates qualitatively unchanged (data not shown).

implies_edges.from: state flagged by the respondent as inappropriately ranked in the cTTO feedback module
implies_edges.to: Utility decrement (β) of an EQ-5D-5L dimension level in the final Danish EQ-5D-5L value set, estimated jointly from cTTO and DCE data

key_assumptions.assumption: Which health states a respondent valued is independent of that respondent's preferences: the EQ-VT assigned each respondent at random to one block of ten cTTO health states (and one of 28 DCE blocks), with randomised ordering.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated design feature of the EQ-VT blocked design (Sect. 2.2.2).

lhs: block of EQ-5D-5L health states assigned to the respondent

implies_edges.to: block of EQ-5D-5L health states assigned to the respondent

key_assumptions.assumption: Hybrid-model key assumption: the parameter vector from the cTTO data equals the parameter vector from the DCE data up to a multiplicative constant (β = β´·θ), with θ allowed to be a function of the explanatory variables.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assessed via plots of the predicted values of the health states from the cTTO (random-effects Tobit) and DCE (conditional logit) parameters: a straight line supports the assumption (Fig. 3).

threats_discussed: Slight under-representation of individuals aged 18-24 years and of individuals with the lowest educational level in the final sample
Change of recruitment source part-way through the study, from the Statistics Denmark sample to a Danish market research company panel
Possible recruitment of 'professional' survey respondents from the market research company panel (excluded if they had taken a health survey within the last 6 months)
Possible interviewer effects (addressed by using a single interview team, intensive training and the EQ-VT quality-control tool)
General difficulty of interpreting health states valued as worse than dead
robustness_checks: Re-estimation after reintroducing the 712 cTTO observations respondents had flagged as incorrectly ranked; estimates qualitatively unchanged (data not shown)
GLS random intercept model without censoring for cTTO data (OSM 3)
Interval regression with heteroscedasticity as a function of observables (gave several significant inconsistencies)
Heteroscedastic conditional logit model for DCE data (similar results, data not shown)
Hybrid model without censoring (OSM 3)
Logical-consistency check of every model's parameter estimates
unresolved_confounders: Under-representation of individuals with the lowest educational level, which the authors state occurred despite their best efforts during data collection
Possible differences between respondents randomly chosen by Statistics Denmark and those recruited from the market research company's panel

estimator.value: Heteroscedastic censored hybrid model (random-effects Tobit for cTTO data combined with a conditional logit for DCE data, scale parameter θ a function of the explanatory variables), regular dummies; Stata 16.1. Marked "Preferred model" in Table 2

estimation.specification: Value of the EQ-5D-5L health state modelled on 20 dimension-level dummies (levels 2-5 of each of the five dimensions; level 1 omitted), no interaction terms, respondent random intercept. Regular-dummy parameterisation: each parameter is measured against level 1.

ambiguities: statistically_significant is read off the printed 95% CI (it excludes / includes zero); Table 2 prints no p-value for this column.
The paper prints no estimating equation, so functional_form is null; the additive no-interaction structure is recorded as a key assumption instead.

The study has no causal identification design. identification.strategy is recorded as structural_model because the coefficient is a parameter of a utility model fitted to experimentally elicited valuations and used to predict all 3125 health states; "descriptive" would be a defensible alternative reading.

evidence.how: Estimation sample: Sect. 3.2 (p. 583) states that removal of the 712 health states respondents identified as incorrectly ranked left 9428 observations for cTTO modelling; Sect. 3.3 (p. 584) states the DCE gave 7098 observations from the same 1014 respondents, and the hybrid model combines the two data sets.

value.claimed_domain: The preferences of the Danish general population; the value set is put forward as key input for healthcare decision-making in a Danish context (QALY estimation for priority setting of hospital-dispensed medicines).
boundary_conditions: The authors note that cross-national differences in the ranking of dimensions might limit the transferability of value sets across countries, suggesting the relevance of country-specific valuation studies.

theory_referenced: episodic random utility model unifying TTO and DCE

falsification.condition: A model was rejected if its parameter estimates were not logically consistent, i.e. if the absolute value of a parameter associated with a logically worse dimension level was not higher than that associated with a logically better level; the GLS, interval-regression, conditional logit and cTTO-only Tobit models were rejected on this criterion.

outcomes_examined_not_reported: Heteroscedastic conditional logit model for the DCE data (data not shown)
Sensitivity analysis reintroducing the 712 incorrectly ranked cTTO states (data not shown)
Experimental DCE valuation task (reported separately)
Questions on attitudes towards prioritisation in the Danish healthcare system (reported separately)
GLS random intercept model, conditional logit model and hybrid model without censoring (reported only in Online Supplementary Material 3)

anchor_quote.text: Beta coefficients should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life

claims.statement: In the heteroscedastic censored hybrid model chosen for the Danish EQ-5D-5L value set, mobility at level 5 carries a utility decrement of 0.22 relative to level 1.

treatment.label: mo5: mobility at level 5 of the EQ-5D-5L health state being valued (regular dummy, level 1 omitted)

definition.value: Regular dummy equal to 1 when the EQ-5D-5L health state presented to the respondent has the mobility dimension at severity level 5; the omitted category is level 1 (no problems) on that dimension. The EQ-5D-5L has five dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) each with five severity levels.

timing.value: Presented to the respondent during the computer-assisted personal interview (October 2018 - November 2019); each respondent valued ten cTTO health states and seven DCE pairs in one interview.

outcome.label: Utility decrement (β) of an EQ-5D-5L dimension level in the final Danish EQ-5D-5L value set, estimated jointly from cTTO and DCE data

definition.value: Table 2 reports β coefficients that "should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life"; a health state's value is 1 minus the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels (worked example, p. 586: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439). The underlying elicited quantity is the observed composite time trade-off value of the health state, on a scale from − 1 to 1 in 0.05 increments (1 = full health, 0 = dead), censored at − 1; the model is estimated on heteroscedastic censored hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data, the model chosen for the final Danish value set.

timing.value: Elicited in the valuation interview itself; the cTTO task values living ten years in the health state, with lead-time TTO adding a further ten years for states considered worse than dead.

units.value: EQ-5D-5L utility decrement, in units of the value scale on which 1 = full health and 0 = dead

magnitude.interpretation: the largest decrement in the 5L value set was for anxiety/depression followed by pain/discomfort and then mobility; mobility level 5 (0.220) is far below pain/discomfort level 5 (0.537) (p. 586)

estimand.target_population: The adult (18+) Danish general population, whose preferences the value set is intended to represent.

population.description: 1014 adults (18+) from the Danish general population interviewed in the Danish EQ-5D-5L valuation study, each valuing ten EQ-5D-5L health states by cTTO and seven pairs by DCE.
population.selection: Statistics Denmark drew a randomly chosen sample representative on age (> 18 years), gender, education and geographical region and supplied contact information on 4585 individuals, invited in blocks of about 500; a Danish market research company panel was added half-way through, selecting respondents by the same principles and excluding anyone who had taken a health survey in the previous 6 months. Of 1052 interviews carried out, 5 were dropped with two interviewers, 12 for software issues/withdrawn consent/cognitive or emotional issues and 21 for not contributing both cTTO and DCE data, leaving 1014.

identification.source_of_variation: Experimental variation in the EQ-5D-5L health states respondents were asked to value: a standardized blocked EQ-VT design in which 86 health states were valued in blocks of ten by cTTO (and 196 pairs in 28 blocks of seven by DCE), with respondents randomly assigned to a block and randomised order of states.

anchor_quote.text: Beta coefficients should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life

claims.statement: In the heteroscedastic censored hybrid model chosen for the Danish EQ-5D-5L value set, usual activity at level 2 carries a utility decrement of 0.033 relative to level 1.

treatment.label: ua2: usual activity at level 2 of the EQ-5D-5L health state being valued (regular dummy, level 1 omitted)

definition.value: Regular dummy equal to 1 when the EQ-5D-5L health state presented to the respondent has the usual activity dimension at severity level 2; the omitted category is level 1 (no problems) on that dimension. The EQ-5D-5L has five dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) each with five severity levels.

timing.value: Presented to the respondent during the computer-assisted personal interview (October 2018 - November 2019); each respondent valued ten cTTO health states and seven DCE pairs in one interview.

outcome.label: Utility decrement (β) of an EQ-5D-5L dimension level in the final Danish EQ-5D-5L value set, estimated jointly from cTTO and DCE data

definition.value: Table 2 reports β coefficients that "should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life"; a health state's value is 1 minus the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels (worked example, p. 586: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439). The underlying elicited quantity is the observed composite time trade-off value of the health state, on a scale from − 1 to 1 in 0.05 increments (1 = full health, 0 = dead), censored at − 1; the model is estimated on heteroscedastic censored hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data, the model chosen for the final Danish value set.

timing.value: Elicited in the valuation interview itself; the cTTO task values living ten years in the health state, with lead-time TTO adding a further ten years for states considered worse than dead.

units.value: EQ-5D-5L utility decrement, in units of the value scale on which 1 = full health and 0 = dead

estimand.target_population: The adult (18+) Danish general population, whose preferences the value set is intended to represent.

population.description: 1014 adults (18+) from the Danish general population interviewed in the Danish EQ-5D-5L valuation study, each valuing ten EQ-5D-5L health states by cTTO and seven pairs by DCE.
population.selection: Statistics Denmark drew a randomly chosen sample representative on age (> 18 years), gender, education and geographical region and supplied contact information on 4585 individuals, invited in blocks of about 500; a Danish market research company panel was added half-way through, selecting respondents by the same principles and excluding anyone who had taken a health survey in the previous 6 months. Of 1052 interviews carried out, 5 were dropped with two interviewers, 12 for software issues/withdrawn consent/cognitive or emotional issues and 21 for not contributing both cTTO and DCE data, leaving 1014.

identification.source_of_variation: Experimental variation in the EQ-5D-5L health states respondents were asked to value: a standardized blocked EQ-VT design in which 86 health states were valued in blocks of ten by cTTO (and 196 pairs in 28 blocks of seven by DCE), with respondents randomly assigned to a block and randomised order of states.

key_assumptions.assumption: Additive main-effects specification: the value of a health state is the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels, with no interactions between dimensions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the EQ-VT was designed for maximum power to identify main effects and that no interaction effects were included or investigated; the worked example on p. 586 adds decrements across dimensions. Not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The censoring of observed cTTO values at − 1, imposed by the construction of the EQ-VT, is correctly handled by the censored (Tobit) specification, and the distributional assumptions of that model hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5.1; the paper argues the Tobit model is conceptually preferred to the GLS model for this reason. The distributional form is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents' stated cTTO valuations measure the preferences of the adult Danish general population, and the achieved sample is representative of that population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 compares the study sample with Statistics Denmark figures for the adult Danish general population on gender, age, marital status, education, work status, income and region; the paper concedes slight under-representation of 18-24-year-olds and of the lowest educational level.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on respondent behaviour: cTTO observations for health states a respondent flagged in the feedback module as inappropriately ranked were dropped (712 observations), and respondents who did not contribute both cTTO and DCE data (n = 21) were dropped.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5 and Sect. 3.2. A sensitivity analysis reintroducing the 712 flagged observations left the estimates qualitatively unchanged (data not shown).

implies_edges.to: Utility decrement (β) of an EQ-5D-5L dimension level in the final Danish EQ-5D-5L value set, estimated jointly from cTTO and DCE data

key_assumptions.assumption: Which health states a respondent valued is independent of that respondent's preferences: the EQ-VT assigned each respondent at random to one block of ten cTTO health states (and one of 28 DCE blocks), with randomised ordering.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated design feature of the EQ-VT blocked design (Sect. 2.2.2).

implies_edges.to: block of EQ-5D-5L health states assigned to the respondent

anchor_quote.text: Beta coefficients should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life

claims.statement: In the heteroscedastic censored hybrid model chosen for the Danish EQ-5D-5L value set, usual activity at level 5 carries a utility decrement of 0.174 relative to level 1.

treatment.label: ua5: usual activity at level 5 of the EQ-5D-5L health state being valued (regular dummy, level 1 omitted)

definition.value: Regular dummy equal to 1 when the EQ-5D-5L health state presented to the respondent has the usual activity dimension at severity level 5; the omitted category is level 1 (no problems) on that dimension. The EQ-5D-5L has five dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) each with five severity levels.

timing.value: Presented to the respondent during the computer-assisted personal interview (October 2018 - November 2019); each respondent valued ten cTTO health states and seven DCE pairs in one interview.

outcome.label: Utility decrement (β) of an EQ-5D-5L dimension level in the final Danish EQ-5D-5L value set, estimated jointly from cTTO and DCE data

definition.value: Table 2 reports β coefficients that "should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life"; a health state's value is 1 minus the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels (worked example, p. 586: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439). The underlying elicited quantity is the observed composite time trade-off value of the health state, on a scale from − 1 to 1 in 0.05 increments (1 = full health, 0 = dead), censored at − 1; the model is estimated on heteroscedastic censored hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data, the model chosen for the final Danish value set.

timing.value: Elicited in the valuation interview itself; the cTTO task values living ten years in the health state, with lead-time TTO adding a further ten years for states considered worse than dead.

units.value: EQ-5D-5L utility decrement, in units of the value scale on which 1 = full health and 0 = dead

estimand.target_population: The adult (18+) Danish general population, whose preferences the value set is intended to represent.

population.description: 1014 adults (18+) from the Danish general population interviewed in the Danish EQ-5D-5L valuation study, each valuing ten EQ-5D-5L health states by cTTO and seven pairs by DCE.
population.selection: Statistics Denmark drew a randomly chosen sample representative on age (> 18 years), gender, education and geographical region and supplied contact information on 4585 individuals, invited in blocks of about 500; a Danish market research company panel was added half-way through, selecting respondents by the same principles and excluding anyone who had taken a health survey in the previous 6 months. Of 1052 interviews carried out, 5 were dropped with two interviewers, 12 for software issues/withdrawn consent/cognitive or emotional issues and 21 for not contributing both cTTO and DCE data, leaving 1014.

claims.statement: In the heteroscedastic censored hybrid model chosen for the Danish EQ-5D-5L value set, anxiety/depression at level 2 carries a utility decrement of 0.072 relative to level 1.

treatment.label: ad2: anxiety/depression at level 2 of the EQ-5D-5L health state being valued (regular dummy, level 1 omitted)

definition.value: Regular dummy equal to 1 when the EQ-5D-5L health state presented to the respondent has the anxiety/depression dimension at severity level 2; the omitted category is level 1 (no problems) on that dimension. The EQ-5D-5L has five dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) each with five severity levels.

timing.value: Presented to the respondent during the computer-assisted personal interview (October 2018 - November 2019); each respondent valued ten cTTO health states and seven DCE pairs in one interview.

outcome.label: Utility decrement (β) of an EQ-5D-5L dimension level in the final Danish EQ-5D-5L value set, estimated jointly from cTTO and DCE data

definition.value: Table 2 reports β coefficients that "should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life"; a health state's value is 1 minus the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels (worked example, p. 586: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439). The underlying elicited quantity is the observed composite time trade-off value of the health state, on a scale from − 1 to 1 in 0.05 increments (1 = full health, 0 = dead), censored at − 1; the model is estimated on heteroscedastic censored hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data, the model chosen for the final Danish value set.

timing.value: Elicited in the valuation interview itself; the cTTO task values living ten years in the health state, with lead-time TTO adding a further ten years for states considered worse than dead.

units.value: EQ-5D-5L utility decrement, in units of the value scale on which 1 = full health and 0 = dead

estimand.target_population: The adult (18+) Danish general population, whose preferences the value set is intended to represent.

population.description: 1014 adults (18+) from the Danish general population interviewed in the Danish EQ-5D-5L valuation study, each valuing ten EQ-5D-5L health states by cTTO and seven pairs by DCE.
population.selection: Statistics Denmark drew a randomly chosen sample representative on age (> 18 years), gender, education and geographical region and supplied contact information on 4585 individuals, invited in blocks of about 500; a Danish market research company panel was added half-way through, selecting respondents by the same principles and excluding anyone who had taken a health survey in the previous 6 months. Of 1052 interviews carried out, 5 were dropped with two interviewers, 12 for software issues/withdrawn consent/cognitive or emotional issues and 21 for not contributing both cTTO and DCE data, leaving 1014.

identification.source_of_variation: Experimental variation in the EQ-5D-5L health states respondents were asked to value: a standardized blocked EQ-VT design in which 86 health states were valued in blocks of ten by cTTO (and 196 pairs in 28 blocks of seven by DCE), with respondents randomly assigned to a block and randomised order of states.

key_assumptions.assumption: Additive main-effects specification: the value of a health state is the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels, with no interactions between dimensions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the EQ-VT was designed for maximum power to identify main effects and that no interaction effects were included or investigated; the worked example on p. 586 adds decrements across dimensions. Not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The censoring of observed cTTO values at − 1, imposed by the construction of the EQ-VT, is correctly handled by the censored (Tobit) specification, and the distributional assumptions of that model hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5.1; the paper argues the Tobit model is conceptually preferred to the GLS model for this reason. The distributional form is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents' stated cTTO valuations measure the preferences of the adult Danish general population, and the achieved sample is representative of that population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 compares the study sample with Statistics Denmark figures for the adult Danish general population on gender, age, marital status, education, work status, income and region; the paper concedes slight under-representation of 18-24-year-olds and of the lowest educational level.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on respondent behaviour: cTTO observations for health states a respondent flagged in the feedback module as inappropriately ranked were dropped (712 observations), and respondents who did not contribute both cTTO and DCE data (n = 21) were dropped.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5 and Sect. 3.2. A sensitivity analysis reintroducing the 712 flagged observations left the estimates qualitatively unchanged (data not shown).

anchor_quote.text: Beta coefficients should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life

claims.statement: In the heteroscedastic censored hybrid model chosen for the Danish EQ-5D-5L value set, anxiety/depression at level 5 carries a utility decrement of 0.618 relative to level 1.

treatment.label: ad5: anxiety/depression at level 5 of the EQ-5D-5L health state being valued (regular dummy, level 1 omitted)

definition.value: Regular dummy equal to 1 when the EQ-5D-5L health state presented to the respondent has the anxiety/depression dimension at severity level 5; the omitted category is level 1 (no problems) on that dimension. The EQ-5D-5L has five dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) each with five severity levels.

timing.value: Presented to the respondent during the computer-assisted personal interview (October 2018 - November 2019); each respondent valued ten cTTO health states and seven DCE pairs in one interview.

outcome.label: Utility decrement (β) of an EQ-5D-5L dimension level in the final Danish EQ-5D-5L value set, estimated jointly from cTTO and DCE data

definition.value: Table 2 reports β coefficients that "should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life"; a health state's value is 1 minus the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels (worked example, p. 586: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439). The underlying elicited quantity is the observed composite time trade-off value of the health state, on a scale from − 1 to 1 in 0.05 increments (1 = full health, 0 = dead), censored at − 1; the model is estimated on heteroscedastic censored hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data, the model chosen for the final Danish value set.

timing.value: Elicited in the valuation interview itself; the cTTO task values living ten years in the health state, with lead-time TTO adding a further ten years for states considered worse than dead.

units.value: EQ-5D-5L utility decrement, in units of the value scale on which 1 = full health and 0 = dead

magnitude.interpretation: the largest utility decrement in the Danish 5L value set; "anxiety/depression was the dimension assigned most value by respondents" (p. 579)

estimand.target_population: The adult (18+) Danish general population, whose preferences the value set is intended to represent.

population.description: 1014 adults (18+) from the Danish general population interviewed in the Danish EQ-5D-5L valuation study, each valuing ten EQ-5D-5L health states by cTTO and seven pairs by DCE.
population.selection: Statistics Denmark drew a randomly chosen sample representative on age (> 18 years), gender, education and geographical region and supplied contact information on 4585 individuals, invited in blocks of about 500; a Danish market research company panel was added half-way through, selecting respondents by the same principles and excluding anyone who had taken a health survey in the previous 6 months. Of 1052 interviews carried out, 5 were dropped with two interviewers, 12 for software issues/withdrawn consent/cognitive or emotional issues and 21 for not contributing both cTTO and DCE data, leaving 1014.

identification.source_of_variation: Experimental variation in the EQ-5D-5L health states respondents were asked to value: a standardized blocked EQ-VT design in which 86 health states were valued in blocks of ten by cTTO (and 196 pairs in 28 blocks of seven by DCE), with respondents randomly assigned to a block and randomised order of states.

claims.statement: In the heteroscedastic censored hybrid model, moving from level 2 to level 3 of mobility adds 0.013 to the utility decrement. The paper states this estimate is not significantly different from the estimate for the preceding level.

treatment.label: mo3: mobility at level 3 relative to level 2 of the same dimension (incremental dummy)

definition.value: Incremental dummy for the mobility dimension: the parameter measures the step from level 2 to level 3 of mobility in the EQ-5D-5L health state being valued. Table 2 reports the hybrid model in both an incremental-dummy and a regular-dummy parameterisation; the regular dummy for mo3 is the sum of the increments up to level 3.

timing.value: Presented to the respondent during the computer-assisted personal interview (October 2018 - November 2019); each respondent valued ten cTTO health states and seven DCE pairs in one interview.

outcome.label: Increment in the utility decrement (β) when moving from the preceding level to this level of the dimension, estimated jointly from cTTO and DCE data

definition.value: Table 2 reports β coefficients that "should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life"; a health state's value is 1 minus the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels (worked example, p. 586: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439). The underlying elicited quantity is the observed composite time trade-off value of the health state, on a scale from − 1 to 1 in 0.05 increments (1 = full health, 0 = dead), censored at − 1; the model is estimated on heteroscedastic censored hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data, reported with incremental dummies so that each parameter is the increment relative to the preceding level of the same dimension.

timing.value: Elicited in the valuation interview itself; the cTTO task values living ten years in the health state, with lead-time TTO adding a further ten years for states considered worse than dead.

units.value: EQ-5D-5L utility decrement, in units of the value scale on which 1 = full health and 0 = dead

estimand.target_population: The adult (18+) Danish general population, whose preferences the value set is intended to represent.

population.description: 1014 adults (18+) from the Danish general population interviewed in the Danish EQ-5D-5L valuation study, each valuing ten EQ-5D-5L health states by cTTO and seven pairs by DCE.
population.selection: Statistics Denmark drew a randomly chosen sample representative on age (> 18 years), gender, education and geographical region and supplied contact information on 4585 individuals, invited in blocks of about 500; a Danish market research company panel was added half-way through, selecting respondents by the same principles and excluding anyone who had taken a health survey in the previous 6 months. Of 1052 interviews carried out, 5 were dropped with two interviewers, 12 for software issues/withdrawn consent/cognitive or emotional issues and 21 for not contributing both cTTO and DCE data, leaving 1014.

identification.source_of_variation: Experimental variation in the EQ-5D-5L health states respondents were asked to value: a standardized blocked EQ-VT design in which 86 health states were valued in blocks of ten by cTTO (and 196 pairs in 28 blocks of seven by DCE), with respondents randomly assigned to a block and randomised order of states.

key_assumptions.assumption: Additive main-effects specification: the value of a health state is the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels, with no interactions between dimensions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the EQ-VT was designed for maximum power to identify main effects and that no interaction effects were included or investigated; the worked example on p. 586 adds decrements across dimensions. Not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The censoring of observed cTTO values at − 1, imposed by the construction of the EQ-VT, is correctly handled by the censored (Tobit) specification, and the distributional assumptions of that model hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5.1; the paper argues the Tobit model is conceptually preferred to the GLS model for this reason. The distributional form is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents' stated cTTO valuations measure the preferences of the adult Danish general population, and the achieved sample is representative of that population.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on respondent behaviour: cTTO observations for health states a respondent flagged in the feedback module as inappropriately ranked were dropped (712 observations), and respondents who did not contribute both cTTO and DCE data (n = 21) were dropped.

claims.statement: In the heteroscedastic censored hybrid model, moving from level 1 to level 2 of self-care adds 0.035 to the utility decrement.

treatment.label: sc2: self-care at level 2 relative to level 1 of the same dimension (incremental dummy)

definition.value: Incremental dummy for the self-care dimension: the parameter measures the step from level 1 to level 2 of self-care in the EQ-5D-5L health state being valued. Table 2 reports the hybrid model in both an incremental-dummy and a regular-dummy parameterisation; the regular dummy for sc2 is the sum of the increments up to level 2.

timing.value: Presented to the respondent during the computer-assisted personal interview (October 2018 - November 2019); each respondent valued ten cTTO health states and seven DCE pairs in one interview.

outcome.label: Increment in the utility decrement (β) when moving from the preceding level to this level of the dimension, estimated jointly from cTTO and DCE data

definition.value: Table 2 reports β coefficients that "should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life"; a health state's value is 1 minus the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels (worked example, p. 586: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439). The underlying elicited quantity is the observed composite time trade-off value of the health state, on a scale from − 1 to 1 in 0.05 increments (1 = full health, 0 = dead), censored at − 1; the model is estimated on heteroscedastic censored hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data, reported with incremental dummies so that each parameter is the increment relative to the preceding level of the same dimension.

timing.value: Elicited in the valuation interview itself; the cTTO task values living ten years in the health state, with lead-time TTO adding a further ten years for states considered worse than dead.

units.value: EQ-5D-5L utility decrement, in units of the value scale on which 1 = full health and 0 = dead

estimand.target_population: The adult (18+) Danish general population, whose preferences the value set is intended to represent.

population.description: 1014 adults (18+) from the Danish general population interviewed in the Danish EQ-5D-5L valuation study, each valuing ten EQ-5D-5L health states by cTTO and seven pairs by DCE.
population.selection: Statistics Denmark drew a randomly chosen sample representative on age (> 18 years), gender, education and geographical region and supplied contact information on 4585 individuals, invited in blocks of about 500; a Danish market research company panel was added half-way through, selecting respondents by the same principles and excluding anyone who had taken a health survey in the previous 6 months. Of 1052 interviews carried out, 5 were dropped with two interviewers, 12 for software issues/withdrawn consent/cognitive or emotional issues and 21 for not contributing both cTTO and DCE data, leaving 1014.

identification.source_of_variation: Experimental variation in the EQ-5D-5L health states respondents were asked to value: a standardized blocked EQ-VT design in which 86 health states were valued in blocks of ten by cTTO (and 196 pairs in 28 blocks of seven by DCE), with respondents randomly assigned to a block and randomised order of states.

key_assumptions.assumption: Additive main-effects specification: the value of a health state is the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels, with no interactions between dimensions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the EQ-VT was designed for maximum power to identify main effects and that no interaction effects were included or investigated; the worked example on p. 586 adds decrements across dimensions. Not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The censoring of observed cTTO values at − 1, imposed by the construction of the EQ-VT, is correctly handled by the censored (Tobit) specification, and the distributional assumptions of that model hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5.1; the paper argues the Tobit model is conceptually preferred to the GLS model for this reason. The distributional form is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents' stated cTTO valuations measure the preferences of the adult Danish general population, and the achieved sample is representative of that population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 compares the study sample with Statistics Denmark figures for the adult Danish general population on gender, age, marital status, education, work status, income and region; the paper concedes slight under-representation of 18-24-year-olds and of the lowest educational level.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on respondent behaviour: cTTO observations for health states a respondent flagged in the feedback module as inappropriately ranked were dropped (712 observations), and respondents who did not contribute both cTTO and DCE data (n = 21) were dropped.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5 and Sect. 3.2. A sensitivity analysis reintroducing the 712 flagged observations left the estimates qualitatively unchanged (data not shown).

claims.statement: In the heteroscedastic censored hybrid model, moving from level 4 to level 5 of self-care adds 0.065 to the utility decrement.

treatment.label: sc5: self-care at level 5 relative to level 4 of the same dimension (incremental dummy)

definition.value: Incremental dummy for the self-care dimension: the parameter measures the step from level 4 to level 5 of self-care in the EQ-5D-5L health state being valued. Table 2 reports the hybrid model in both an incremental-dummy and a regular-dummy parameterisation; the regular dummy for sc5 is the sum of the increments up to level 5.

timing.value: Presented to the respondent during the computer-assisted personal interview (October 2018 - November 2019); each respondent valued ten cTTO health states and seven DCE pairs in one interview.

outcome.label: Increment in the utility decrement (β) when moving from the preceding level to this level of the dimension, estimated jointly from cTTO and DCE data

definition.value: Table 2 reports β coefficients that "should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life"; a health state's value is 1 minus the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels (worked example, p. 586: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439). The underlying elicited quantity is the observed composite time trade-off value of the health state, on a scale from − 1 to 1 in 0.05 increments (1 = full health, 0 = dead), censored at − 1; the model is estimated on heteroscedastic censored hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data, reported with incremental dummies so that each parameter is the increment relative to the preceding level of the same dimension.

timing.value: Elicited in the valuation interview itself; the cTTO task values living ten years in the health state, with lead-time TTO adding a further ten years for states considered worse than dead.

units.value: EQ-5D-5L utility decrement, in units of the value scale on which 1 = full health and 0 = dead

estimand.target_population: The adult (18+) Danish general population, whose preferences the value set is intended to represent.

population.description: 1014 adults (18+) from the Danish general population interviewed in the Danish EQ-5D-5L valuation study, each valuing ten EQ-5D-5L health states by cTTO and seven pairs by DCE.
population.selection: Statistics Denmark drew a randomly chosen sample representative on age (> 18 years), gender, education and geographical region and supplied contact information on 4585 individuals, invited in blocks of about 500; a Danish market research company panel was added half-way through, selecting respondents by the same principles and excluding anyone who had taken a health survey in the previous 6 months. Of 1052 interviews carried out, 5 were dropped with two interviewers, 12 for software issues/withdrawn consent/cognitive or emotional issues and 21 for not contributing both cTTO and DCE data, leaving 1014.

identification.source_of_variation: Experimental variation in the EQ-5D-5L health states respondents were asked to value: a standardized blocked EQ-VT design in which 86 health states were valued in blocks of ten by cTTO (and 196 pairs in 28 blocks of seven by DCE), with respondents randomly assigned to a block and randomised order of states.

key_assumptions.assumption: Additive main-effects specification: the value of a health state is the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels, with no interactions between dimensions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the EQ-VT was designed for maximum power to identify main effects and that no interaction effects were included or investigated; the worked example on p. 586 adds decrements across dimensions. Not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The censoring of observed cTTO values at − 1, imposed by the construction of the EQ-VT, is correctly handled by the censored (Tobit) specification, and the distributional assumptions of that model hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5.1; the paper argues the Tobit model is conceptually preferred to the GLS model for this reason. The distributional form is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents' stated cTTO valuations measure the preferences of the adult Danish general population, and the achieved sample is representative of that population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 compares the study sample with Statistics Denmark figures for the adult Danish general population on gender, age, marital status, education, work status, income and region; the paper concedes slight under-representation of 18-24-year-olds and of the lowest educational level.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on respondent behaviour: cTTO observations for health states a respondent flagged in the feedback module as inappropriately ranked were dropped (712 observations), and respondents who did not contribute both cTTO and DCE data (n = 21) were dropped.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5 and Sect. 3.2. A sensitivity analysis reintroducing the 712 flagged observations left the estimates qualitatively unchanged (data not shown).

claims.statement: In the heteroscedastic censored hybrid model, moving from level 3 to level 4 of usual activity adds 0.099 to the utility decrement.

treatment.label: ua4: usual activity at level 4 relative to level 3 of the same dimension (incremental dummy)

definition.value: Incremental dummy for the usual activity dimension: the parameter measures the step from level 3 to level 4 of usual activity in the EQ-5D-5L health state being valued. Table 2 reports the hybrid model in both an incremental-dummy and a regular-dummy parameterisation; the regular dummy for ua4 is the sum of the increments up to level 4.

timing.value: Presented to the respondent during the computer-assisted personal interview (October 2018 - November 2019); each respondent valued ten cTTO health states and seven DCE pairs in one interview.

definition.value: Table 2 reports β coefficients that "should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life"; a health state's value is 1 minus the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels (worked example, p. 586: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439). The underlying elicited quantity is the observed composite time trade-off value of the health state, on a scale from − 1 to 1 in 0.05 increments (1 = full health, 0 = dead), censored at − 1; the model is estimated on heteroscedastic censored hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data, reported with incremental dummies so that each parameter is the increment relative to the preceding level of the same dimension.

timing.value: Elicited in the valuation interview itself; the cTTO task values living ten years in the health state, with lead-time TTO adding a further ten years for states considered worse than dead.

units.value: EQ-5D-5L utility decrement, in units of the value scale on which 1 = full health and 0 = dead

population.description: 1014 adults (18+) from the Danish general population interviewed in the Danish EQ-5D-5L valuation study, each valuing ten EQ-5D-5L health states by cTTO and seven pairs by DCE.
population.selection: Statistics Denmark drew a randomly chosen sample representative on age (> 18 years), gender, education and geographical region and supplied contact information on 4585 individuals, invited in blocks of about 500; a Danish market research company panel was added half-way through, selecting respondents by the same principles and excluding anyone who had taken a health survey in the previous 6 months. Of 1052 interviews carried out, 5 were dropped with two interviewers, 12 for software issues/withdrawn consent/cognitive or emotional issues and 21 for not contributing both cTTO and DCE data, leaving 1014.

identification.source_of_variation: Experimental variation in the EQ-5D-5L health states respondents were asked to value: a standardized blocked EQ-VT design in which 86 health states were valued in blocks of ten by cTTO (and 196 pairs in 28 blocks of seven by DCE), with respondents randomly assigned to a block and randomised order of states.

key_assumptions.assumption: Additive main-effects specification: the value of a health state is the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels, with no interactions between dimensions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the EQ-VT was designed for maximum power to identify main effects and that no interaction effects were included or investigated; the worked example on p. 586 adds decrements across dimensions. Not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The censoring of observed cTTO values at − 1, imposed by the construction of the EQ-VT, is correctly handled by the censored (Tobit) specification, and the distributional assumptions of that model hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5.1; the paper argues the Tobit model is conceptually preferred to the GLS model for this reason. The distributional form is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents' stated cTTO valuations measure the preferences of the adult Danish general population, and the achieved sample is representative of that population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 compares the study sample with Statistics Denmark figures for the adult Danish general population on gender, age, marital status, education, work status, income and region; the paper concedes slight under-representation of 18-24-year-olds and of the lowest educational level.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on respondent behaviour: cTTO observations for health states a respondent flagged in the feedback module as inappropriately ranked were dropped (712 observations), and respondents who did not contribute both cTTO and DCE data (n = 21) were dropped.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5 and Sect. 3.2. A sensitivity analysis reintroducing the 712 flagged observations left the estimates qualitatively unchanged (data not shown).

ambiguities: Table 2 prints the P value as "0.000"; it is recorded as 0.0 with p_value_relation "exact" because that is what is printed, but it is a rounded value and the true p-value is only known to be below 0.0005.
The paper prints no estimating equation, so functional_form is null; the additive no-interaction structure is recorded as a key assumption instead.

The study has no causal identification design. identification.strategy is recorded as structural_model because the coefficient is a parameter of a utility model fitted to experimentally elicited valuations and used to predict all 3125 health states; "descriptive" would be a defensible alternative reading.

evidence.how: Estimation sample: Sect. 3.2 (p. 583) states that removal of the 712 health states respondents identified as incorrectly ranked left 9428 observations for cTTO modelling; Sect. 3.3 (p. 584) states the DCE gave 7098 observations from the same 1014 respondents, and the hybrid model combines the two data sets.

theory_referenced: episodic random utility model unifying TTO and DCE

falsification.condition: A model was rejected if its parameter estimates were not logically consistent, i.e. if the absolute value of a parameter associated with a logically worse dimension level was not higher than that associated with a logically better level; the GLS, interval-regression, conditional logit and cTTO-only Tobit models were rejected on this criterion.

claims.statement: In the heteroscedastic censored hybrid model, moving from level 2 to level 3 of pain/discomfort adds 0.045 to the utility decrement.

treatment.label: pd3: pain/discomfort at level 3 relative to level 2 of the same dimension (incremental dummy)

definition.value: Incremental dummy for the pain/discomfort dimension: the parameter measures the step from level 2 to level 3 of pain/discomfort in the EQ-5D-5L health state being valued. Table 2 reports the hybrid model in both an incremental-dummy and a regular-dummy parameterisation; the regular dummy for pd3 is the sum of the increments up to level 3.

timing.value: Presented to the respondent during the computer-assisted personal interview (October 2018 - November 2019); each respondent valued ten cTTO health states and seven DCE pairs in one interview.

outcome.label: Increment in the utility decrement (β) when moving from the preceding level to this level of the dimension, estimated jointly from cTTO and DCE data

definition.value: Table 2 reports β coefficients that "should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life"; a health state's value is 1 minus the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels (worked example, p. 586: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439). The underlying elicited quantity is the observed composite time trade-off value of the health state, on a scale from − 1 to 1 in 0.05 increments (1 = full health, 0 = dead), censored at − 1; the model is estimated on heteroscedastic censored hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data, reported with incremental dummies so that each parameter is the increment relative to the preceding level of the same dimension.

timing.value: Elicited in the valuation interview itself; the cTTO task values living ten years in the health state, with lead-time TTO adding a further ten years for states considered worse than dead.

units.value: EQ-5D-5L utility decrement, in units of the value scale on which 1 = full health and 0 = dead

claims.statement: In the random-effects Tobit model of cTTO data, mobility at level 3 carries a utility decrement of 0.061 relative to level 1. The paper states this estimate is not significantly different from the estimate for the preceding level.

treatment.label: mo3: mobility at level 3 of the EQ-5D-5L health state being valued (regular dummy, level 1 omitted)

definition.value: Regular dummy equal to 1 when the EQ-5D-5L health state presented to the respondent has the mobility dimension at severity level 3; the omitted category is level 1 (no problems) on that dimension. The EQ-5D-5L has five dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) each with five severity levels.

timing.value: Presented to the respondent during the computer-assisted personal interview (October 2018 - November 2019); each respondent valued ten cTTO health states and seven DCE pairs in one interview.

outcome.label: Utility decrement (β) of an EQ-5D-5L dimension level, estimated from the observed composite time trade-off (cTTO) value of the health state

definition.value: Table 2 reports β coefficients that "should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life"; a health state's value is 1 minus the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels (worked example, p. 586: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439). The underlying elicited quantity is the observed composite time trade-off value of the health state, on a scale from − 1 to 1 in 0.05 increments (1 = full health, 0 = dead), censored at − 1; the model is estimated on random-effects Tobit model estimated on the cTTO data alone, which takes explicit account of the censoring of observed cTTO values at − 1.

timing.value: Elicited in the valuation interview itself; the cTTO task values living ten years in the health state, with lead-time TTO adding a further ten years for states considered worse than dead.

units.value: EQ-5D-5L utility decrement, in units of the value scale on which 1 = full health and 0 = dead

estimand.target_population: The adult (18+) Danish general population, whose preferences the value set is intended to represent.

population.description: 1014 adults (18+) from the Danish general population interviewed in the Danish EQ-5D-5L valuation study, each valuing ten EQ-5D-5L health states by cTTO and seven pairs by DCE.
population.selection: Statistics Denmark drew a randomly chosen sample representative on age (> 18 years), gender, education and geographical region and supplied contact information on 4585 individuals, invited in blocks of about 500; a Danish market research company panel was added half-way through, selecting respondents by the same principles and excluding anyone who had taken a health survey in the previous 6 months. Of 1052 interviews carried out, 5 were dropped with two interviewers, 12 for software issues/withdrawn consent/cognitive or emotional issues and 21 for not contributing both cTTO and DCE data, leaving 1014.

identification.source_of_variation: Experimental variation in the EQ-5D-5L health states respondents were asked to value: a standardized blocked EQ-VT design in which 86 health states were valued in blocks of ten by cTTO (and 196 pairs in 28 blocks of seven by DCE), with respondents randomly assigned to a block and randomised order of states.

key_assumptions.assumption: Additive main-effects specification: the value of a health state is the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels, with no interactions between dimensions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the EQ-VT was designed for maximum power to identify main effects and that no interaction effects were included or investigated; the worked example on p. 586 adds decrements across dimensions. Not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The censoring of observed cTTO values at − 1, imposed by the construction of the EQ-VT, is correctly handled by the censored (Tobit) specification, and the distributional assumptions of that model hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5.1; the paper argues the Tobit model is conceptually preferred to the GLS model for this reason. The distributional form is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents' stated cTTO valuations measure the preferences of the adult Danish general population, and the achieved sample is representative of that population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 compares the study sample with Statistics Denmark figures for the adult Danish general population on gender, age, marital status, education, work status, income and region; the paper concedes slight under-representation of 18-24-year-olds and of the lowest educational level.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on respondent behaviour: cTTO observations for health states a respondent flagged in the feedback module as inappropriately ranked were dropped (712 observations), and respondents who did not contribute both cTTO and DCE data (n = 21) were dropped.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5 and Sect. 3.2. A sensitivity analysis reintroducing the 712 flagged observations left the estimates qualitatively unchanged (data not shown).

claims.statement: In the random-effects Tobit model of cTTO data, self-care at level 2 carries a utility decrement of 0.03 relative to level 1. The paper states this estimate is not significantly different from the estimate for the preceding level.

treatment.label: sc2: self-care at level 2 of the EQ-5D-5L health state being valued (regular dummy, level 1 omitted)

definition.value: Regular dummy equal to 1 when the EQ-5D-5L health state presented to the respondent has the self-care dimension at severity level 2; the omitted category is level 1 (no problems) on that dimension. The EQ-5D-5L has five dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) each with five severity levels.

timing.value: Presented to the respondent during the computer-assisted personal interview (October 2018 - November 2019); each respondent valued ten cTTO health states and seven DCE pairs in one interview.

outcome.label: Utility decrement (β) of an EQ-5D-5L dimension level, estimated from the observed composite time trade-off (cTTO) value of the health state

definition.value: Table 2 reports β coefficients that "should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life"; a health state's value is 1 minus the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels (worked example, p. 586: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439). The underlying elicited quantity is the observed composite time trade-off value of the health state, on a scale from − 1 to 1 in 0.05 increments (1 = full health, 0 = dead), censored at − 1; the model is estimated on random-effects Tobit model estimated on the cTTO data alone, which takes explicit account of the censoring of observed cTTO values at − 1.

timing.value: Elicited in the valuation interview itself; the cTTO task values living ten years in the health state, with lead-time TTO adding a further ten years for states considered worse than dead.

units.value: EQ-5D-5L utility decrement, in units of the value scale on which 1 = full health and 0 = dead

estimand.target_population: The adult (18+) Danish general population, whose preferences the value set is intended to represent.

population.description: 1014 adults (18+) from the Danish general population interviewed in the Danish EQ-5D-5L valuation study, each valuing ten EQ-5D-5L health states by cTTO and seven pairs by DCE.
population.selection: Statistics Denmark drew a randomly chosen sample representative on age (> 18 years), gender, education and geographical region and supplied contact information on 4585 individuals, invited in blocks of about 500; a Danish market research company panel was added half-way through, selecting respondents by the same principles and excluding anyone who had taken a health survey in the previous 6 months. Of 1052 interviews carried out, 5 were dropped with two interviewers, 12 for software issues/withdrawn consent/cognitive or emotional issues and 21 for not contributing both cTTO and DCE data, leaving 1014.

identification.source_of_variation: Experimental variation in the EQ-5D-5L health states respondents were asked to value: a standardized blocked EQ-VT design in which 86 health states were valued in blocks of ten by cTTO (and 196 pairs in 28 blocks of seven by DCE), with respondents randomly assigned to a block and randomised order of states.

key_assumptions.assumption: Additive main-effects specification: the value of a health state is the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels, with no interactions between dimensions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the EQ-VT was designed for maximum power to identify main effects and that no interaction effects were included or investigated; the worked example on p. 586 adds decrements across dimensions. Not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: The censoring of observed cTTO values at − 1, imposed by the construction of the EQ-VT, is correctly handled by the censored (Tobit) specification, and the distributional assumptions of that model hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5.1; the paper argues the Tobit model is conceptually preferred to the GLS model for this reason. The distributional form is not tested.

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents' stated cTTO valuations measure the preferences of the adult Danish general population, and the achieved sample is representative of that population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 compares the study sample with Statistics Denmark figures for the adult Danish general population on gender, age, marital status, education, work status, income and region; the paper concedes slight under-representation of 18-24-year-olds and of the lowest educational level.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on respondent behaviour: cTTO observations for health states a respondent flagged in the feedback module as inappropriately ranked were dropped (712 observations), and respondents who did not contribute both cTTO and DCE data (n = 21) were dropped.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5 and Sect. 3.2. A sensitivity analysis reintroducing the 712 flagged observations left the estimates qualitatively unchanged (data not shown).

claims.statement: In the random-effects Tobit model of cTTO data, self-care at level 5 carries a utility decrement of 0.172 relative to level 1.

treatment.label: sc5: self-care at level 5 of the EQ-5D-5L health state being valued (regular dummy, level 1 omitted)

definition.value: Regular dummy equal to 1 when the EQ-5D-5L health state presented to the respondent has the self-care dimension at severity level 5; the omitted category is level 1 (no problems) on that dimension. The EQ-5D-5L has five dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) each with five severity levels.

timing.value: Presented to the respondent during the computer-assisted personal interview (October 2018 - November 2019); each respondent valued ten cTTO health states and seven DCE pairs in one interview.

outcome.label: Utility decrement (β) of an EQ-5D-5L dimension level, estimated from the observed composite time trade-off (cTTO) value of the health state

definition.value: Table 2 reports β coefficients that "should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life"; a health state's value is 1 minus the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels (worked example, p. 586: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439). The underlying elicited quantity is the observed composite time trade-off value of the health state, on a scale from − 1 to 1 in 0.05 increments (1 = full health, 0 = dead), censored at − 1; the model is estimated on random-effects Tobit model estimated on the cTTO data alone, which takes explicit account of the censoring of observed cTTO values at − 1.

timing.value: Elicited in the valuation interview itself; the cTTO task values living ten years in the health state, with lead-time TTO adding a further ten years for states considered worse than dead.

units.value: EQ-5D-5L utility decrement, in units of the value scale on which 1 = full health and 0 = dead

estimand.target_population: The adult (18+) Danish general population, whose preferences the value set is intended to represent.

population.description: 1014 adults (18+) from the Danish general population interviewed in the Danish EQ-5D-5L valuation study, each valuing ten EQ-5D-5L health states by cTTO and seven pairs by DCE.
population.selection: Statistics Denmark drew a randomly chosen sample representative on age (> 18 years), gender, education and geographical region and supplied contact information on 4585 individuals, invited in blocks of about 500; a Danish market research company panel was added half-way through, selecting respondents by the same principles and excluding anyone who had taken a health survey in the previous 6 months. Of 1052 interviews carried out, 5 were dropped with two interviewers, 12 for software issues/withdrawn consent/cognitive or emotional issues and 21 for not contributing both cTTO and DCE data, leaving 1014.

identification.source_of_variation: Experimental variation in the EQ-5D-5L health states respondents were asked to value: a standardized blocked EQ-VT design in which 86 health states were valued in blocks of ten by cTTO (and 196 pairs in 28 blocks of seven by DCE), with respondents randomly assigned to a block and randomised order of states.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Sect. 2.5.1; the paper argues the Tobit model is conceptually preferred to the GLS model for this reason. The distributional form is not tested.

anchor_quote.text: Beta coefficients should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life

claims.statement: In the random-effects Tobit model of cTTO data, usual activity at level 4 carries a utility decrement of 0.153 relative to level 1.

treatment.label: ua4: usual activity at level 4 of the EQ-5D-5L health state being valued (regular dummy, level 1 omitted)

definition.value: Regular dummy equal to 1 when the EQ-5D-5L health state presented to the respondent has the usual activity dimension at severity level 4; the omitted category is level 1 (no problems) on that dimension. The EQ-5D-5L has five dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) each with five severity levels.

timing.value: Presented to the respondent during the computer-assisted personal interview (October 2018 - November 2019); each respondent valued ten cTTO health states and seven DCE pairs in one interview.

outcome.label: Utility decrement (β) of an EQ-5D-5L dimension level, estimated from the observed composite time trade-off (cTTO) value of the health state

definition.value: Table 2 reports β coefficients that "should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life"; a health state's value is 1 minus the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels (worked example, p. 586: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439). The underlying elicited quantity is the observed composite time trade-off value of the health state, on a scale from − 1 to 1 in 0.05 increments (1 = full health, 0 = dead), censored at − 1; the model is estimated on random-effects Tobit model estimated on the cTTO data alone, which takes explicit account of the censoring of observed cTTO values at − 1.

timing.value: Elicited in the valuation interview itself; the cTTO task values living ten years in the health state, with lead-time TTO adding a further ten years for states considered worse than dead.

units.value: EQ-5D-5L utility decrement, in units of the value scale on which 1 = full health and 0 = dead

estimand.target_population: The adult (18+) Danish general population, whose preferences the value set is intended to represent.

population.description: 1014 adults (18+) from the Danish general population interviewed in the Danish EQ-5D-5L valuation study, each valuing ten EQ-5D-5L health states by cTTO and seven pairs by DCE.
population.selection: Statistics Denmark drew a randomly chosen sample representative on age (> 18 years), gender, education and geographical region and supplied contact information on 4585 individuals, invited in blocks of about 500; a Danish market research company panel was added half-way through, selecting respondents by the same principles and excluding anyone who had taken a health survey in the previous 6 months. Of 1052 interviews carried out, 5 were dropped with two interviewers, 12 for software issues/withdrawn consent/cognitive or emotional issues and 21 for not contributing both cTTO and DCE data, leaving 1014.

identification.source_of_variation: Experimental variation in the EQ-5D-5L health states respondents were asked to value: a standardized blocked EQ-VT design in which 86 health states were valued in blocks of ten by cTTO (and 196 pairs in 28 blocks of seven by DCE), with respondents randomly assigned to a block and randomised order of states.

claims.statement: In the random-effects Tobit model of cTTO data, pain/discomfort at level 3 carries a utility decrement of 0.077 relative to level 1.

treatment.label: pd3: pain/discomfort at level 3 of the EQ-5D-5L health state being valued (regular dummy, level 1 omitted)

definition.value: Regular dummy equal to 1 when the EQ-5D-5L health state presented to the respondent has the pain/discomfort dimension at severity level 3; the omitted category is level 1 (no problems) on that dimension. The EQ-5D-5L has five dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) each with five severity levels.

timing.value: Presented to the respondent during the computer-assisted personal interview (October 2018 - November 2019); each respondent valued ten cTTO health states and seven DCE pairs in one interview.

outcome.label: Utility decrement (β) of an EQ-5D-5L dimension level, estimated from the observed composite time trade-off (cTTO) value of the health state

definition.value: Table 2 reports β coefficients that "should be read as utility decrements in the calculation of health-related quality of life"; a health state's value is 1 minus the sum of the decrements of its dimension levels (worked example, p. 586: state 13224 has U = 1-0-0.050-0.033-0.048-0.430 = 0.439). The underlying elicited quantity is the observed composite time trade-off value of the health state, on a scale from − 1 to 1 in 0.05 increments (1 = full health, 0 = dead), censored at − 1; the model is estimated on random-effects Tobit model estimated on the cTTO data alone, which takes explicit account of the censoring of observed cTTO values at − 1.

timing.value: Elicited in the valuation interview itself; the cTTO task values living ten years in the health state, with lead-time TTO adding a further ten years for states considered worse than dead.

units.value: EQ-5D-5L utility decrement, in units of the value scale on which 1 = full health and 0 = dead

ambiguities: statistically_significant is read off the printed 95% CI (it excludes / includes zero); Table 2 prints no p-value for this column.
This column is the cTTO-only model, which the paper did not choose for the final value set; the heteroscedastic censored hybrid model (the third column of Table 2) is marked "Preferred model".
